posts.title: Korean Ramen Pots: Is the Aluminium One Safe?

images.alt: A gold anodised aluminium Korean ramyun pot with two gold side handles, a matching gold lid and a black knob, lit against a dark background.
images.caption: This is the pot the word 양은냄비 actually calls to mind — gold, not silver, and made of anodised aluminium. Photo by The Marmot, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

images.alt: Chart: the Gyeonggi Institute of Health and Environment tested 56 aluminium pots sold in Korea by boiling citric acid at pH 3.5. The 47 uncoated pots leached 23.90 mg/L of aluminium on average with a highest single reading of 115.21 mg/L; the 9 coated pots averaged 1.78 mg/L with a highest of 8.72, about thirteen times less. By dish, kimchi jjigae leached 9.86 mg per kg, pickles 2.86, kimchi ramyun 2.34 and doenjang jjigae 1.64.
images.caption: The study that answers the question, and does not exist in English. Chart by EpicKor.

images.alt: Kimchi ramyun simmering in a metal pot on a stovetop, wavy noodles and kimchi visible in a red broth, with a Korean instant noodle packet in the background.
images.caption: The exact combination the study measured: kimchi, acid, salt and a thin metal pot. Photo by makafood via Pexels.

images.alt: Chart in three parts: never use a metal scourer, because one pass with a steel scrubber takes the protective film off, so use a soft sponge and wooden utensils; do not store food in it, because salty acidic stew left sitting corrodes the pot, so transfer to a bowl as soon as cooking finishes; and when to throw it out — visible discolouration or scratches, with Korean guidance putting daily-use replacement at six months to a year.
images.caption: Every number above assumes the film is intact. Chart by EpicKor.

images.alt: Rabokki — tteokbokki rice cakes cooked together with ramyun noodles in a red spicy broth — bubbling in a plain metal pot on a red table.
images.caption: Rabokki in the same pot. Gochujang-based broth sits on the acidic side, which is precisely the case the study was measuring. Photo by Theodore Nguyen via Pexels.
